newsitem.title: UK: Legal & General sees FTSE peak in Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: Legal & General sees FTSE peak in Q1 1997.

text.p: The UK's FTSE 100 index will set record highs in the first quarter of next year but will boil over and end 1997 little different from its current levels, according to a strategy note from Legal & General Investment Management.

Writing in L&G's monthly "Fundamentals" bulletin, director David Shaw said he expected the FTSE to rise as high as 4,400 in the first quarter of 1997 before dropping to around 3,800 and ending the year at around 4,000.
At 1436 GMT on Friday it stood at 3,981.2.
That is just over 100 points short of the intraday record 4,094.4 set on November 26.

Shaw said he expected conventional UK government gilts to produce a return of around zero next year, while commercial property would be the best performing asset with a return of between 12 percent and 14 percent on the year.
"Some time in the first quarter of 1997 we are expecting FTSE to attain its peak for the year," Shaw said.

"We would not rule out a level of 4,400. At that level, however, the dividend yield will be sub 3.6 percent which, on the only two previous occasions when this did prevail, was soon followed by a correction."
"This could be triggered by a number of events -- a sell-off on Wall Street, the calling of the UK general election, or a backup in global bond yields."

Shaw said L&G expects two quarter-point rises in UK interest rates before the election to cool expanding economic growth, followed by a swift one percent rise after the poll, which he expects to see the return of a Labour government.
He expects corporate earnings to grow by betwwen eight and ten percent during 1997, though Labour's promised windfall tax on utilities will reduce that to between five and seven percent.

The appeal of UK equities will further be reduced by a five percent reduction in the tax that can be reclaimed by pension funds on companies' advance corporation tax, Shaw said -- reducing the dividend yield by about 25 basis points.
Shaw said the 1997 outlook for UK equities was problematic because of uncertainties over the precise timing and outcome of the general election and the risk of a general market setback.
However in the first quarter of next year Shaw expects markets to make further progress on the back of benign inflation, low interest rates and a modest acceleration in world business activity.
"Pro tem, we are continuing our modest overweight position in UK equities," he said. "We remain fully invested overall."
